400.title: The youngest (1 Samuel 16)
400.hook: man sees the face, but the Lord beholdeth the heart; David is out with the sheep
400.carry: the lord looks at the heart
400.howItsDone: Catholics hear David's anointing at Mass, including on the Fourth Sunday of Lent in one year of the cycle, and Catholic preaching turns to it when speaking of how God chooses the humble and overlooked.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saul, head and shoulders above everyone, hiding in the baggage on the day he was chosen. Your line was hiding in the baggage.

Four hundred days in, and today is about being overlooked. Saul's reign has gone wrong, and God sends old Samuel to Bethlehem with a horn of oil, to the house of a man named Jesse, Isai in the Douay-Rheims. One of Jesse's sons will be the next king. Jesse lines them up. The oldest, Eliab, walks in first, and he looks the part: tall, strong, the kind of man you'd cast as a king. Samuel thinks, surely this is the one. After all, the last king was chosen standing head and shoulders above the crowd.
screen: `A HORN OF OIL TO BETHLEHEM.` → `JESSE LINES UP HIS SONS.` → `SURELY THIS IS THE ONE.`

segments.voice: And God stops him. In the Douay-Rheims: "Look not on his countenance, nor on the height of his stature." Then the line the whole chapter is built on: "man seeth those things that appear, but the Lord beholdeth the heart." Notice the dig at height: yesterday the crowd cheered a king for being tall. So the parade goes on. Seven sons pass in front of Samuel, and each time the answer is the same: the Lord hath not chosen this one. Samuel is puzzled. Are these all your sons? And Jesse says, almost as an afterthought: there's the youngest. He's out keeping the sheep. Nobody thought to call him in. Samuel says: we won't sit down until he comes. They fetch him. And the text, honestly, says he was good-looking too, ruddy and handsome. God's choice isn't against beauty; it just isn't based on it. The Lord says: arise, anoint him, for this is he. Samuel pours the oil in the middle of his brothers, and the Spirit of the Lord comes upon David from that day on. The pattern keeps coming back in the Bible: the younger brother, the overlooked one, the shepherd. Catholics see it run all the way to Bethlehem again, where the son of David is born among shepherds, and to Mary's song: "He hath put down the mighty from their seat, and hath exalted the humble."

segments.voice: Walk in your mind through a room you'll be in soon, a family dinner, the pew at Sunday Mass, and find the one out in the field: the quiet one, the new one, the one who always does the dishes. Wonder what they might be carrying, or what they're good at that nobody has asked about. If you pray, ask to see them the way the Lord sees, at the heart.
The youngest. David, Jesse's eighth son, left out in the fields with the sheep, and the one God chose because the Lord looks at the heart. Today's word.
Your line: the lord looks at the heart. Height was never the measure. Four hundred days now, and i'm glad you're here.

401.title: Five smooth stones (1 Samuel 17)
401.hook: a shepherd refuses the king's armor and faces a giant
401.howItsDone: Catholics hear the story of David and Goliath in the weekday Mass readings, and Catholic schools and youth programs tell it as a story of trusting God and using the gifts you've been given.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the youngest, called in from the sheep and anointed among his brothers. Your line was the lord looks at the heart.

Two armies face each other across a valley, and for forty days nobody moves. Every morning and every evening, a champion walks out from the Philistine side and shouts: send me one man. If he beats me, we'll serve you. Goliath of Gath. Huge, in a bronze helmet and a coat of mail, with a spear like a weaver's beam. And every morning Israel's army, King Saul included, stays put, afraid. Then Jesse's youngest son shows up from Bethlehem with grain and loaves for his older brothers. He hears the shouting and asks: who is this, to defy the armies of the living God?
screen: `TWO ARMIES, ONE VALLEY.` → `FORTY DAYS OF SHOUTING.` → `A BOY BRINGS BREAD TO HIS BROTHERS.`

segments.voice: David offers to fight. Saul says what anyone would: you're a boy, and he's been a warrior since his youth. David answers with his résumé: I keep my father's sheep. When a lion or a bear took a lamb, I went after it. The Lord who saved me from the lion will save me from this Philistine. So Saul says go, and kindly dresses David in his own armor, a bronze helmet, a coat of mail, the king's sword. David clanks a few steps and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I cannot go thus, for I am not used to it." He takes it all off. Instead he picks up his staff, a sling, and "five smooth stones out of the brook," dropped into his shepherd's bag. Tools he knows. Goliath sees a young man with a stick and is insulted: am I a dog? David's answer is the center of the story: "Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the Lord of hosts." One stone, slung, and the giant falls on his face. The story is about trust: the battle is the Lord's, David says, not won by sword and spear. And it's about being yourself. Saul's armor was a gift, kindly meant; it just wasn't his. David doesn't win as a smaller copy of Saul. He fights as a shepherd, with a shepherd's things, and that's enough.

402.title: David and Jonathan (1 Samuel 18–20)
402.hook: a prince loves David as his own soul and warns him with arrows
402.howItsDone: Catholics hear part of the David and Jonathan story at weekday Mass early in Ordinary Time, in one year of the two-year cycle (1 Samuel 18–19).

segments.voice: Yesterday, Goliath, and a shepherd who took off the king's armor. Your line was not in borrowed armor.

On paper, these two should be rivals. One is Jonathan, King Saul's son and heir, a brave soldier in his own right. The other is David, who just killed Goliath. After the battle the women of Israel come out dancing with a song: Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands. Saul hears it and something sours in him. From that day, the text says, he keeps a jealous eye on David. Jonathan is the one who stands to lose a kingdom. Instead, something else happens.
screen: `A PRINCE AND A SHEPHERD.` → `HIS THOUSANDS, DAVID'S TEN THOUSANDS.` → `A KING GROWS JEALOUS.`

segments.voice: It begins in one sentence, in the Douay-Rheims: "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." Knit. The Hebrew verb means tied or bound together, the word for a knot. The two make a covenant, a solemn promise before God. And Jonathan seals it with a gesture: he takes off his own robe and gives it to David, then his armor, his sword, his bow and his belt. The heir to the throne hands the shepherd the clothes of a prince. Then Saul's jealousy turns murderous. He throws a spear at David and orders his servants to kill him. Jonathan is caught between his father and his friend. He doesn't pretend the danger isn't real, and he abandons neither of them. He speaks up for David to his father's face, and his father hurls a spear at him too. Then comes the plan with the arrows. David hides in a field. Jonathan goes out to shoot with a boy. If he calls, the arrows are on this side of you, David is safe. If he calls, the arrows are beyond you, David must run. Jonathan shoots, and calls out: the arrow is beyond thee. The boy runs off with the arrows, knowing nothing. The two friends meet, kiss and weep, David most of all. They part with a promise: the Lord be between me and thee for ever. In the twelfth century, the English abbot Aelred of Rievaulx held these two up in his book on spiritual friendship: loyal when it costs a crown, honest when it's dangerous, and bound before God.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a friend who stood by you when it cost them something, who spoke up for you in a room you weren't in, or stayed when leaving was easier. Picture their face, remember one specific thing they did, and let yourself feel how much it mattered. If you pray, thank God for them by name.

403.title: The cave (1 Samuel 24)
403.hook: David could kill Saul and cuts only his robe
403.howItsDone: Catholics hear David's mercy to Saul in the weekday Mass readings, and the Church reads it alongside Jesus's teaching to love one's enemies and not repay evil for evil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, David and Jonathan's nefesh, and the arrow that flew beyond the boy. Your line was knit to his soul.

David is now a fugitive. King Saul has taken three thousand chosen men into the wild country near En-gedi, rocks so steep only wild goats climb them, to hunt him down. David and his men are hiding deep in a cave. And of all the caves in the desert, Saul walks into theirs. Alone. He's come in, the text says politely, to ease nature. He has no idea who is sitting a few yards behind him in the dark. David's men lean in and whisper: this is the day the Lord promised. Your enemy, delivered into your hand.
screen: `THREE THOUSAND MEN HUNTING DAVID.` → `SAUL WALKS INTO THEIR CAVE.` → `THIS IS THE DAY.`

segments.voice: David creeps forward in the dark, close enough to strike, and secretly cuts off the hem of Saul's robe. That's all. And then, the Douay-Rheims says, "David's heart struck him." Even that small cut bothers his conscience. He stops his men from going any further: Saul is still, in David's words, the Lord's anointed. Saul walks out of the cave and goes on his way, never knowing how close it was. Then David takes a real risk. He steps out after him and calls: My lord the king! Saul turns around. David bows to the ground before the man trying to kill him, holds up the piece of cloth, and calls him my father. I had a thought to kill thee, "but my eye hath spared thee. For I said: I will not put out my hand against my lord." I will not. That's the whole story in three words. David has a reason, an opportunity, and men cheering him on. He also has the one thing that matters more: a line he won't cross. And for a moment, it breaks Saul open. "Is this thy voice, my son David?" Saul weeps out loud, and says: "Thou art more just than I." It doesn't last. Saul will hunt David again. Mercy doesn't always change the other person. But it changes who David is. Catholic readers see in this cave an early picture of what Jesus will ask: not repaying evil for evil, even when you could, even when everyone around you says you should.

segments.voice: Think of someone who has hurt you, and who, honestly, you could hurt back: a secret you know, a comment you could make, a forward button, a group chat. Put yourself in the cave with the chance right in front of you, let it go by, and say quietly David's three words: I will not. If you pray, ask for the strength to keep that line.

404.title: Dancing before the ark (2 Samuel 6)
404.hook: David dances with all his might and his wife despises him
404.howItsDone: In the Litany of Loreto, Catholics call on Mary as Ark of the Covenant, and the Vigil Mass of the Assumption reads the Chronicles account of David bringing the ark into Jerusalem.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cave, and a hem cut from a king's robe instead of his life. Your line was I will not.

Saul is gone now, and David is king in Jerusalem. He sets out to bring the ark of God into his city: the gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the law, the place Israel knew as God's throne among them. The first attempt goes badly. The ark rides on a new cart, the oxen stumble, a man named Uzzah reaches out to steady it, and he dies on the spot. David is shaken. How shall the ark of the Lord come to me? he asks. He leaves it at the house of a man named Obed-edom, and it stays there three months.
screen: `DAVID WANTS THE ARK IN JERUSALEM.` → `THE OXEN STUMBLE.` → `HOW SHALL THE ARK COME TO ME?`

segments.voice: Then word comes that God has blessed Obed-edom's whole household because of the ark. So David tries again, this time with joy. After six steps he offers a sacrifice. Trumpets, shouting, the whole city in the street. And the king, the Douay-Rheims says, "danced with all his might before the Lord." Not a dignified sway. Leaping, whirling, dressed only in a simple linen ephod, a priest's garment, not his royal robes. Up at a window, someone is watching: Michal, David's wife, Saul's daughter. And she "despised him in her heart." When he comes home she lets him have it: how glorious the king of Israel was today, uncovering himself in front of the servant girls like some fool. David's answer is the heart of the story. It was before the Lord, he says, and "I will be little in my own eyes." He'll look foolish again if that's what praise costs. Catholics read this chapter beside a second story. In Luke's Gospel, Mary travels to the hill country of Judah to visit her cousin Elizabeth. Elizabeth cries out, why should the mother of my Lord come to me? It echoes David's question about the ark. The baby John leaps in Elizabeth's womb, the way David leapt before the ark. And Mary stays three months, as the ark stayed three months in that house. Catholic tradition draws these threads together and calls Mary the Ark of the Covenant, the one who carried God's presence. You'll hear that title in the Litany of Loreto.

405.title: Thou art the man (2 Samuel 11–12)
405.hook: adultery, murder, and a prophet's story that makes the king see himself
405.carry: I have sinned against the Lord
405.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 51 (50 in the Douay numbering), the Miserere, at Morning Prayer on Fridays in the Liturgy of the Hours, and some use it to prepare for the sacrament of confession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, David dancing before the ark with all his might. Your line was dance anyway. Today, the same king at his lowest.

It's the turn of the year, when kings go out to war. David sends his army and stays home. One afternoon he walks on the palace roof and sees a woman bathing. Bathsheba, Bethsabee in the Douay-Rheims, the wife of Uriah, one of his own soldiers, away at the front. David sends for her. He's the king; nobody refuses the king. She becomes pregnant. To hide it, David brings Uriah home, but the loyal soldier won't sleep in comfort while his comrades are in tents. So David writes a letter, has Uriah carry it himself, and it says: put him at the front, and pull back.
screen: `THE KING STAYS HOME FROM WAR.` → `A WOMAN SEEN FROM THE ROOF.` → `A LETTER CARRIED BY ITS VICTIM.`

segments.voice: Uriah dies. David marries Bathsheba. Then God sends the prophet Nathan, who doesn't accuse. He tells a story. Two men in one city. One rich, with flocks and herds. One poor, with one little ewe lamb, which, the Douay says, grew up with his children, ate from his plate, drank from his cup, slept in his arms, and "was unto him as a daughter." A traveler visits the rich man, who doesn't take from his own flocks. He takes the poor man's lamb and serves it for dinner. David is furious. The man who did this deserves to die! He'll pay it back four times over! And Nathan says four words: "Thou art the man." David could see the injustice clearly as long as it was somebody else. The parable gets past his defenses, then turns around. And David, who holds all the power in the room, doesn't kill the prophet or spin it. He says, "I have sinned against the Lord." Nathan answers: the Lord hath taken away thy sin. The consequences still come; the chapters ahead are full of grief in David's house. But Nathan's word stands. Tradition gives this moment a song. The Douay's Psalm fifty, the Miserere, has a heading that sets it here, when Nathan came to David. It begins: "Have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy." The Church prays it in the Liturgy of the Hours, and Catholics bring its spirit into confession: say it plainly, and hear the word of pardon.

segments.voice: Think of who could be your Nathan, someone who'd tell you the truth to your face, and what pattern they might name that you spot in others and not in yourself. 406.title: My son Absalom (2 Samuel 18:33)
406.hook: the rebellious son dies and David wishes he had died instead
406.carry: would god I had died for thee
406.howItsDone: Catholics hear Absalom's rebellion and David's grief in the weekday Mass readings, and Catholics pray for divided families at Mass and in the rosary, some asking the intercession of Saint Monica, honored as a patron of parents with wayward children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nathan's story of the little ewe lamb, and four words to a king. Your line was I have sinned against the Lord.

Nathan warned David that trouble would rise from inside his own house, and it does. Years of it. A terrible wrong between his children, a revenge killing, a son sent into exile, then brought home but kept at arm's length. That son is Absalom, handsome and famous for his thick hair. He sits by the city gate, listens to people's complaints, and tells them: if only I were judge, you'd get justice. Slowly he wins the hearts of Israel. Then he declares himself king, and David has to flee Jerusalem on foot, weeping as he climbs the Mount of Olives. Father and son are now at war.
screen: `TROUBLE FROM INSIDE THE HOUSE.` → `ABSALOM AT THE CITY GATE.` → `DAVID FLEES JERUSALEM, WEEPING.`

segments.voice: The armies meet in a forest. Before the battle, David gives his commanders one order, in front of everyone, and the Douay-Rheims puts it tenderly: "Save me the boy Absalom." The boy. A grown man leading a rebellion to take his father's throne, and David still calls him the boy. The battle goes against Absalom. Riding a mule under a great oak, his head catches in the branches, the mule runs on, and he's left hanging between heaven and earth. David's commander Joab finds him and, against the king's order, kills him. Messengers run to David, who is waiting between the city gates. The first is vague. The second says it plainly: may all the king's enemies be as that young man is. And David breaks. He climbs to the room above the gate, weeping: my son Absalom, Absalom my son, and in the Douay-Rheims: "would to God that I might die for thee." Older English Bibles put it as would God I had died for thee. Count how many times he says my son. He has won the war and lost his child, and he would rather have died himself. Some Christian readers hear something more in that cry: a father who would die in place of a rebellious son. David could only wish it. For them, in Christ, God did it. And that's week fifty-eight: a shepherd chosen, a giant, a friend, a cave, a dance, a confession, and a father's grief.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a family that's split, maybe yours: a parent and child who don't speak, siblings who stopped sharing a table. Don't try to solve it; just hold them, the way David held Absalom's name in the middle of a war. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, simply wish them peace.
Absalom. The rebel son David still called the boy, and cried over, wishing he had died in his place. Today's word.
